course.title: Java Beginner Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive beginner course for the Java programming language. Covers variables, data types, OOP, collections, exception handling, file I/O, generics, lambdas, streams, and a capstone project. Designed for complete beginners with detailed explanations that gradually become more concise.

blocks.value: What is Java?

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995 and is now owned by Oracle. Java's motto is 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) — compiled Java code runs on any platform that has a Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
Where is Java Used?

Java powers a massive portion of the software world:
• Enterprise Applications: Banking systems, insurance platforms, ERP systems (Spring, Jakarta EE)
• Android Development: Native Android apps are built with Java (and Kotlin)
• Web Backend: Spring Boot is the most popular Java framework for REST APIs
• Big Data: Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark, Kafka are Java-based
• Cloud Services: Netflix, Amazon, LinkedIn use Java for microservices
• Desktop Applications: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, Minecraft
• Embedded Systems: Smart cards, IoT devices, set-top boxes
How Java Differs from Other Languages

Java vs Python: Java is statically typed and compiled, Python is dynamically typed and interpreted. Java is faster for large applications; Python is faster to write small scripts.

Java vs C++: Java has automatic memory management (garbage collection), C++ requires manual memory management. Java runs on a VM; C++ compiles to native machine code.

Java vs JavaScript: Completely different languages despite similar names. Java is compiled and strongly typed; JavaScript is interpreted and dynamically typed.

Java vs Rust: Java has a garbage collector and simpler memory model; Rust uses ownership for memory safety without GC. Java has a larger ecosystem; Rust has better performance for systems programming.
Why Top Companies Choose Java

Companies like Google, Amazon, Netflix, Uber, Spotify, and banks worldwide use Java because:
• Mature Ecosystem: 30+ years of libraries, frameworks, and tooling
• Strong Typing: Catches errors at compile time, reducing runtime bugs
• JVM Performance: JIT compilation makes Java surprisingly fast
• Massive Talent Pool: Easy to hire Java developers globally
• Enterprise-Grade: Built-in security, concurrency, and monitoring
• Backward Compatibility: Code written in Java 1.0 still runs today
• Spring Ecosystem: Spring Boot makes building microservices incredibly productive

blocks.value: Handling Errors Gracefully

Exceptions are events that disrupt the normal flow of program execution. Java uses a structured exception handling mechanism with try, catch, finally, throw, and throws. Exceptions are objects that extend the Throwable class hierarchy.

• Error: Serious problems you shouldn't catch (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
• Exception: Conditions your program should catch
  - RuntimeException (unchecked): NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
  - Other exceptions (checked): IOException, SQLException

blocks.value: When to Use Which

| Operation | ArrayList | LinkedList |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| Random access (get) | O(1) — Fast | O(n) — Slow |
| Add/remove at end | O(1) amortized | O(1) |
| Add/remove at middle | O(n) | O(n) (but faster in practice for small lists) |
| Add/remove at beginning | O(n) | O(1) |
| Memory overhead | Low | High (pointers) |

Use ArrayList for most cases. Use LinkedList only when you frequently add/remove at the beginning or need queue/stack behavior.

blocks.question: Which List implementation provides O(1) random access?
blocks.explanation: ArrayList uses a backing array, so get(index) is O(1). LinkedList must traverse from the head, making it O(n).

blocks.question: Does List allow duplicate elements?
blocks.explanation: List implementations (ArrayList, LinkedList) allow duplicate elements and maintain insertion order. Use Set if you need uniqueness.

blocks.question: What diamond operator syntax creates a typed ArrayList in Java 7+?
blocks.explanation: The diamond operator <> allows type inference: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); The compiler infers the type from the left side.

blocks.value: Thread Lifecycle

States: NEW (created, not started), RUNNABLE (ready or running), BLOCKED (waiting for monitor lock), WAITING (indefinitely waiting), TIMED_WAITING (waiting with timeout), TERMINATED (completed). Use volatile for visibility and synchronized/locks for atomicity.

blocks.question: What does the synchronized keyword prevent?
blocks.explanation: synchronized ensures only one thread accesses a critical section at a time, preventing race conditions where multiple threads modify shared data simultaneously.

blocks.question: Which is preferred over creating new Thread objects directly?
blocks.explanation: ExecutorService manages a pool of reusable threads, reducing overhead. It provides better resource management, task submission, and graceful shutdown.

blocks.question: What keyword ensures a variable's changes are visible to all threads?

blocks.value: Stack vs Heap

| Feature | Stack | Heap |
|---------|-------|------|
| Stores | Local variables, method calls | Objects and instance variables |
| Size | Small, fixed per thread | Large, shared across threads |
| Lifetime | Method execution | Until garbage collected |
| Speed | Very fast allocation/deallocation | Slower, requires GC |

blocks.value: Project Jigsaw and the Module System

Java 9 introduced the Java Platform Module System (JPMS) to address the monolithic nature of the JDK. Modules enforce strong encapsulation, explicit dependencies, and smaller runtime images. Understanding JPMS is essential for modern Java development, especially when creating custom JREs with jlink.
Creating a Module
Module Descriptor Explained

| Directive | Purpose | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| requires | Depend on another module | requires java.sql; |
| requires transitive | Dependence propagated to consumers | requires transitive java.xml; |
| exports | Make package public to other modules | exports com.api; |
| exports ... to | Export to specific modules only | exports com.internal to com.test; |
| opens | Open package for deep reflection | opens com.model; |
| provides ... with | Register service implementation | provides Logger with FileLogger; |
| uses | Declare service consumption | uses Logger; |

Strong encapsulation means non-exported packages are inaccessible even via reflection (unless opened).
Compiling and Running Modules

# Directory structure:
# project/
#   com.example.app/
#     module-info.java
#     com/example/app/Main.java
#   com.example.lib/
#     module-info.java
#     com/example/lib/Util.java

# Compile modules
javac -d out --module-source-path . $(find . -name '*.java')

# Run a module
java --module-path out -m com.example.app/com.example.app.Main

# Describe a module
java --module-path out --describe-module com.example.app

# List all observable modules
java --module-path out --list-modules

# Create custom JRE with jlink
jlink --module-path out:$JAVA_HOME/jmods \
      --add-modules com.example.app \
      --output my-custom-jre

blocks.value: Unnamed Module and Automatic Modules

• Unnamed Module: Classpath code lives here. It can read all modules but no named module can read it. This is the migration bridge.
• Automatic Module: A JAR on the module path without module-info becomes an automatic module. Its name is derived from the JAR filename, and it exports all packages and reads all other modules.

Migration strategy: 1) Run on classpath (unnamed), 2) Move to module path as automatic module, 3) Add module-info.java.

blocks.value: Reflection Performance Considerations

Reflection is slower than direct code because it bypasses compile-time optimizations. Mitigations:
• Set accessible once, reuse the Field/Method object
• Use MethodHandle (Java 7+) for better performance
• Use VarHandle (Java 9+) for variable access
• Cache reflection results
• In modules, opened packages are required for deep reflection

Modern frameworks use a mix: reflection for discovery, generated bytecode (via ASM or ByteBuddy) for hot paths.

blocks.explanation: PreparedStatement uses parameterized queries, separating SQL code from data. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings with Statement.

blocks.value: Making Java Applications Fast

Performance optimization is about measuring first, then improving. Java provides excellent profiling tools (JVisualVM, async-profiler, JFR) and JVM flags for tuning. Understanding JIT compilation, escape analysis, and common bottlenecks helps you write efficient code without premature optimization.
JIT Compilation and Hotspots

The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode. As methods execute frequently, the JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler compiles hot bytecode to native machine code. The C1 compiler (client) optimizes quickly, while C2 (server) applies aggressive optimizations after more profiling data is collected.

Tiers: 0=Interpreter, 1-3=C1 with increasing profiling, 4=C2 optimized. Methods that fail deoptimization fall back to lower tiers.

blocks.value: Shipping Java to Production

Writing code is only half the battle — deploying, monitoring, and operating Java applications in production requires understanding containers, CI/CD, observability, and cloud-native patterns. This part covers Docker, Kubernetes basics, monitoring with Micrometer, and building native images with GraalVM.
Dockerizing Java Applications

# Multi-stage build for smaller, secure images
# Stage 1: Build
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests

# Stage 2: Runtime
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Create non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -S javauser && adduser -S javauser -G javauser
USER javauser

# Copy only the built JAR
COPY --from=builder /app/target/*.jar app.jar

# JVM tuning for containers
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+UseG1GC"

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]
Spring Boot Docker Support

# Spring Boot 2.3+ has built-in layered JAR support
# pom.xml plugin configuration:
# <configuration>
#   <layers>
#     <enabled>true</enabled>
#   </layers>
# </configuration>

# Build layered JAR
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image

# Or with Cloud Native Buildpacks
pack build myapp --builder paketobuildpacks/builder:base

# Run container
docker run -p 8080:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod myapp:latest

# Docker Compose for local development
# docker-compose.yml:
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/mydb
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
Observability with Micrometer and Actuator
GraalVM Native Images

# Native image compilation (requires GraalVM)
# Benefits: instant startup, low memory, no JIT warmup

# With Spring Boot 3+
./mvnw native:compile

# Or using native-image directly
native-image -cp myapp.jar -H:Name=myapp-native -H:+ReportExceptionStackTraces

# Build arguments for reflection (Spring handles this automatically)
# -H:ReflectionConfigurationFiles=reflect-config.json

# Container-optimized build
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Pnative

# Compare startup times:
# JVM: ~3-5 seconds
# Native: ~0.05 seconds

# Trade-offs:
# - Longer build times
# - No JIT optimizations at runtime
# - Some features unsupported (dynamic bytecode, some reflection)
# - Platform-specific binary
CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions

# .github/workflows/java-ci.yml
name: Java CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Set up JDK 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '21'
          distribution: 'temurin'
          cache: maven
      
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./mvnw clean verify
      
      - name: Generate test report
        uses: dorny/test-reporter@v1
        if: always()
        with:
          name: Maven Tests
          path: target/surefire-reports/*.xml
          reporter: java-junit
      
      - name: Build Docker image
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag myapp:${{ github.sha }} myapp:latest
      
      - name: Run security scan
        uses: anchore/scan-action@v3
        with:
          image: "myapp:latest"
          fail-build: false
Production Checklist

Before deploying Java to production:
• Use a minimal JRE base image (eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine)
• Run as non-root user inside container
• Set appropriate heap limits (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage)
• Enable health checks and readiness probes
• Configure structured logging (JSON format)
• Set up distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Zipkin)
• Monitor JVM metrics (heap, GC, threads)
• Use connection pooling for databases
• Enable HTTPS/TLS termination
• Have rollback strategy and feature flags
• Run dependency vulnerability scans regularly
